content.title: About
content.content: Cuban crackers are crisp, thin biscuits made from wheat flour, vegetable oil, and a pinch of salt. They have a light golden color, delicate texture, and a subtle sweet‑savory flavor typical of traditional Cuban snacks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cuban crackers first appeared in the early 20th century as a way to preserve bread in the hot climate.
They are traditionally served with cheese, avocado, or guacamole.
The original recipe includes a small amount of sugar, giving the crackers a faint sweetness.
Crackers are often used as a base for canapés at parties and buffets.
In Cuba they are commonly called “paneles.”

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Crackers provide slowly digestible carbohydrates that help sustain energy and fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many snack biscuits, Cuban crackers are baked with a modest amount of oil.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour supplies modest amounts of B1, B2, and niacin, which support metabolism.

items.title: Gentle on digestion
items.content: Their light texture makes them easy to digest, suitable as a mild snack during minor stomach upset.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: A small amount of fiber helps maintain regular bowel function.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Made from wheat flour, these crackers are not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Some varieties are salted; those monitoring sodium intake should choose unsalted versions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because they contain simple carbs, crackers can raise blood sugar levels, which is relevant for diabetics.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Commercial versions may contain preservatives or flavor enhancers that some consumers prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cuban crackers can be enjoyed straight from the pack, paired with cheese, ham, avocado, or guacamole, or used as a base for mini‑sandwiches. They also add a pleasant crunch when sprinkled into soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life store them in the refrigerator to prevent oil from going rancid. Discard any that develop a stale or off‑flavor.
